I took the light path: one task writing one file, nothing risky. I read the PDFs, the image and the memo myself, and another agent checked every answer against its source.

| Key | Answer | Source |
|---|---|---|
| q1 | `"BRAMBLE"` | memo.txt line 9: "runs under the project code name BRAMBLE" (Project Larch was the cancelled 2024 plan) |
| q2 | `"2023-03-09"` | report.pdf page 3: "the Lisbon office opened its doors on 9 March 2023" |

| q7 | `450` | manual.pdf page 6: the MX-9 standard interval is 750 operating hours; page 54: dusty sites multiply the interval by 0.6 |

**How q5 was computed:** cell B6 on the Summary sheet is labelled "Net total" and holds `B4+B5`. Following the formulas back to the Lines sheet:
- the lines add up to 15703;
- an 8% discount of 1256.24 leaves 14446.76;
- VAT of 3611.69 brings the total to 18058.45.

Despite the "net" label, the cell includes VAT, so I used the cell's own formula rather than the label. Two agents arrived at this figure separately.

**Why q5 was late:** the agents couldn't run the `unzip` command in this session. Until one of them read the workbook with Python instead, q5 held a placeholder `0` so the file stayed in a valid format.

I implemented all twelve modules, and each one passes its public examples against the real standard library. The per-module runs add up to 111 of 111, but nobody re-ran the whole `python3 tests/run_public.py` once all modules were in place. The hidden tests (about 1,760) were not run, so the score is unknown.

**Path taken:** the full path, sped up for the deadline. A light path was out because there are twelve modules. I split the work into six slices of two modules each. All six ran at the same time in the shared folder, without worktrees, because work left unmerged in a worktree at the deadline would not have been graded. Each slice wrote only its own two files. Nothing was committed.

| Slice | Modules | Public examples passed | Review |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | tomlparse, b64 | 19/19 | pass |
| S2 | fraction, regex | 18/18 | pass (opus) |
| S3 | csvx, cal | 19/19 | pass |
| S4 | ipaddr, wrap | 18/18 | pass (opus) |
| S5 | shellsplit, urls | 19/19 | pass (opus) |
| S6 | diff, jsonx | 18/18 | pass |

S2's first worker couldn't run its test commands. On a second try it installed `fraction.py` but ran out of time for `regex.py`. A fresh worker then wrote `regex.py` from the stub, and both modules passed review.

For the rule against forbidden imports, each review loaded the two modules and checked which modules Python had pulled in. No forbidden module appeared in any slice; S5's review found no imports at all. The only imports in the code are `datetime` in `cal.py` (a worker read SPEC.md as allowing it), `namedtuple` from `collections` in `diff.py`, and `sys` in `regex.py`. Every module imports without errors.

**Limits:**
- **Only public examples were checked.** No review compared each module's full API or its error types with its spec.
- **Python version:** the S5 worker reported that the local Python is 3.15.2, not 3.13, so the public examples compared against 3.15. A few `urls` edge cases may behave differently on 3.13; there it followed the spec.
- **Rushed modules:** `regex.py` was written in about two minutes, so it is the module most likely to lose hidden tests.

I used the full path: twelve independent modules are too much for one session. I split them into six slices of two modules each and ran them in parallel in the shared working tree, not in git worktrees. With a 10-minute limit, work left in an unmerged worktree would not have been graded.

All twelve modules are implemented and in the working tree, nothing is committed, and the last full run of `python3 tests/run_public.py` passed 111 of 111 public examples. One known gap remains: `ndiff` in `toolkit/diff.py` still differs from `difflib.ndiff` on some inputs.

| Slice | Modules | Review | Public examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | `regex`, `b64` | passed | 19/19 |
| S2 | `tomlparse`, `shellsplit` | passed, plus opus review | 18/18 |
| S3 | `diff`, `fraction` | passed opus review; implementer reported a gap | 18/18 |
| S4 | `jsonx`, `cal` | passed, plus opus review | 19/19 |
| S5 | `csvx`, `wrap` | passed | 18/18 |
| S6 | `ipaddr`, `urls` | passed, plus opus review | 19/19 |

**Forbidden imports:** reviewers grepped the imports and checked which modules get loaded. Nothing forbidden is used:
- `regex.py` imports only `sys`.
- `tomlparse.py` and `cal.py` import only `datetime`.
- `diff.py` imports `collections` and `heapq`.
- `fraction.py` imports `math`, `sys` and `decimal`. Loading `decimal` pulls in `numbers`; neither is a reimplemented module. `SPEC.md` doesn't mention either one, and I didn't verify that `decimal` loads none of the twelve indirectly.
- `shellsplit.py`, `b64.py`, `jsonx.py`, `csvx.py`, `wrap.py`, `ipaddr.py` and `urls.py` import nothing.

**Public API:** for S1, S2 and S6, reviewers matched the top-level names in each spec against the code, and all were present. For S4 and S5 the evidence is only that the public examples run; nobody compared the specs name by name.

**What may cost hidden tests:**
- **`diff.ndiff`:** it disagrees with the real `difflib.ndiff` in about 131 of 3,000 random cases, because of how it chooses which pair of similar lines to align. The rest of `diff` and all of `fraction` matched the real modules in the implementer's own tests. I didn't send it back for a fix because time was up, and a half-edited file at the cutoff would have scored the whole module zero.
- **Little testing beyond the public examples:** S1 (`regex`, `b64`), S2 (`tomlparse`, `shellsplit`) and S4 (`jsonx`, `cal`) had their wider comparisons against the real modules blocked when shell commands were refused. Rare edge cases there, especially in `regex`, are untested. S5 (`csvx`, `wrap`) got only a few spot-checks.
- **`ipaddr`:** two cases the spec marks as never tested still differ: a network built with a zone id, and `reverse_pointer` on a network object.
